_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: And Rabbi Yoḥanan follows his line of reasoning: that there is no retroactive designation [ein bereira].
tosafot:a1.1: And Rabbi Yoḥanan follows his line of reasoning, etc.: Here Rabbi Elazar disagrees with Rabbi Yoḥanan, while above, at the end of Yesh Bekhor [52b; the printed reference reads 22b], it is implied that he concedes in that case that they are purchasers, where the Gemara answers: what does “they do not return” mean? They do not return for nothing [i.e., without payment]. This is no contradiction, since here the Gemara treats Rabbi Yoḥanan’s two statements as each necessary [so one may agree about the field and still disagree about tithe]. Alternatively, the answer above was needed only so that that source would not be a difficulty against Rabbi Yoḥanan.
gershom:a1.1: And Rabbi Yoḥanan follows his line of reasoning: he does not accept retroactive designation, and therefore they return [the portions] to each other in the Jubilee, since we do not say: this is the portion that was his due.
rashi:a2.1: And they are necessary: these two statements of Rabbi Yoḥanan.
rashi:a2.2: In this case Rabbi Yoḥanan says: that there is no retroactive designation and they are exempt, because animal tithe is juxtaposed to “your son,” as it is written (Exodus 22:28–29): “The firstborn of your sons you shall give to Me; so shall you do [with your oxen and with your sheep].”
rashi:a2.3: When it is clear to you: that it was born in your possession.
gershom:a2.1: So too your cattle and your sheep, when it is clear to you: that it is your own share, and there is no retroactive designation. But an inherited field, which is not a sale, I might say need not be returned.
rashi:a3.1: And if he had taught us the field: I would have said that it is there that Rabbi Yoḥanan says this, because he goes toward stringency on account of the uncertainty; but here it would be a leniency, since they would be exempt from tithe. Alternatively, “at the beginning”: with the Jubilee we require the land to return to its beginning, when it was held together; but with tithe one cannot say this.
gershom:a3.1: And if he had taught us the field: an inheritance, which they return to each other because they are like purchasers, that is a stringency. But here, with animal tithe, if we treat them as purchasers that is a leniency, since they are exempt from tithe; I might say not.
gershom:a4.1: Alternatively: had he taught us about a field that they are like purchasers and return it, that would be because of “at the beginning”: that is, now when they return [the portions], each one’s share goes back to the other as at the beginning, as it was before the division, and they fulfil the verse “you shall return every man to his possession.” That is why he says there is no retroactive designation, so that they return. But here, with animal tithe, which has no law of return in the Jubilee, I might say there is retroactive designation. It teaches us that there is not.
rashi:a4.1: And similarly partners: [this is taught] in Tractate Temura, in the chapter Kol HaAsurin.
rashi:a4.2: One took ten lambs and one took nine lambs and a dog with them: those ten lambs opposite the dog are forbidden for the altar, since one of them was the dog’s exchange and so is “the price of a dog,” and we do not know which one it is.
rashi:a4.3: Those with the dog: the nine with the dog have no prohibition in them.
tosafot:a4.1: Let him select one of them to correspond to the dog, etc.: And if you ask, what would that help? It is not known which one is opposite the dog. And if you say, the one that is worth as much as the dog: but [Rav Ashi] says, “if they are all equal to each other, indeed” [one may select], and then how can he pick out the one opposite the dog so as to permit the others? One may answer that this is the Gemara’s reasoning: since there is retroactive designation, the matter can depend on his intent, for presumably his intent from the start was that the one he will select is the one opposite the dog.
rashi:a5.1: If they are all equal to each other: every lamb among those nine has a counterpart among the ten worth the same, so the tenth turns out to be opposite the dog. Indeed, there is retroactive designation: he takes one as the price of the dog and eats it, and the rest are permitted for the Most High [the altar].
rashi:a5.2: Here we are dealing with a case where all of them are forbidden, for example where they are not equal to each other: the nine lambs among the ten are worth more than the nine with the dog, and the dog is worth the tenth plus that small amount by which those nine opposite exceed the nine with it. Now the price of the dog runs through all nine opposite it, a little in each, and the tenth is opposite it. And the Teacher reads: for example, where each one is worth four zuz and half a fifth, and the dog five zuz, that one zuz is shared and runs into all of them. The explanation is this: each of the ten opposite the dog is worth four zuz and half a fifth of a zuz, so all ten are worth forty-one zuz, since ten halves of a fifth make five fifths, which is one zuz. The dog is worth five zuz, so the nine with it come to only thirty-six zuz [the printed text reads fifty-six], and with the dog’s five that makes forty-one. Now those with the dog are worth only four zuz each, and those opposite it four zuz and half a fifth each; the dog evens them all out, and the dog’s exchange is shared among all those opposite it: the half-fifth by which each is worth more than four zuz, against the one zuz by which the dog is worth more than four.
gershom:a5.1: Those opposite the dog are forbidden: all ten, since we do not know which is the price of the dog, its exchange. If all ten are equal to each other, each one worth as much as the dog, indeed we say: let him select one opposite the dog.
gershom:a6.1: For this small amount is shared among all ten, and there is no retroactive designation; therefore all those opposite the dog are forbidden for sacrifice.
rashi:a6.1: Mishna. Any whose mother died: at the time of birth. The whole reasoning of the mishna is explained in the Gemara.
rashi:a6.2: And the shelaḥ exists: and the hide exists.
rashi:a6.3: This is not an orphan: the Gemara explains the reason.
tosafot:a6.1: Except for diverse kinds, etc.: It could also have listed an animal that resembles [another kind], since the Gemara explains the reason as being that we derive “under,” “under” from consecrated animals. But everywhere it lists [these], it usually skips the resembling animal, as though it were included in diverse kinds, since it is somewhat like it.
gershom:a7.1: Any whose mother died: when this one was born, or was slaughtered; for the one [the mother] departs toward death and this one toward life.
gershom:a8.1: And the shelaḥ exists: her hide, so that one can wrap it in its mother’s hide and warm it with it; this is not an orphan.
rashi:a7.1: A bull or a sheep: this is written about all the other consecrated animals.
rashi:a7.2: Resembling: whose mother is a ewe and it looks like a goat.
rashi:a7.3: Diverse kinds: it comes from a he-goat and a ewe.
gershom:a9.1: A bull or a sheep: it must be distinctly a bull or a sheep; this excludes diverse kinds.
rashi:a8.1: It is stated here: with animal tithe, “under the rod.”
rashi:a8.2: And it is stated there: with all consecrated animals, “under its mother.”
rashi:a8.3: Just as there: with all consecrated animals.
rashi:a8.4: Excluding all these categories: as I explained, diverse kinds, the resembling animal, one born by caesarean section, one whose time has not arrived, and an orphan; so too with tithe. And that is the reason of the mishna. And just as tithe excludes a tereifa, as it is written of it (Leviticus 27:32), “whatever passes,” excluding a tereifa, which does not pass: an animal whose legs were cut off from the knee [arkhuba] upward, which is one of the eighteen tereifot.
gershom:a10.1: And just as here, with tithe, it excludes a tereifa, as it is written “whatever passes,” excluding a tereifa that does not pass, so too there, with consecrated animals, it excludes a tereifa.
rashi:a9.1: All: which is taught in the mishna; what does it come to include?
rashi:a9.2: Set aside [mukẓe]: one that they set aside to offer to idol worship.
rashi:a9.3: Worshipped: one where he worshipped the animal itself, for example he poured a libation to it between its horns.
gershom:a11.1: A tumtum does not enter: since he holds that it is a creature of its own kind.
rashi:a10.1: And our tanna: the tanna of the mishna, who teaches “all” to include all these [listed in the baraita].
rashi:a10.2: If he derives: tithe from consecrated animals, through “under,” “under.”
rashi:a10.3: These too should not [enter]: for all of them are disqualified as offerings, as is taught in Temura, in the chapter Kol HaAsurin (Temura 28a): “from the cattle” excludes the animal that copulated with a person and the one that was the object of bestiality, where there is only one witness to the matter, for with two witnesses it is liable to death, as it is written, “and you shall kill the animal”; “from the herd” excludes the worshipped animal; “from the flock” excludes the one set aside.
rashi:a10.4: And if he does not derive: from consecrated animals, then these others, one whose time has not arrived and an orphan, from where does he know that they are not tithed?
gershom:a12.1: And if he does not derive: these very ones that he excludes, from where does he know them?
rashi:a11.1: And these: the animal that copulated, the one that was the object, and all the rest. The Merciful One included them to be tithed, and even though they are unfit to be sacrificed, they are eaten by their owners with their blemish.
rashi:a13.1: Wherever a blemish disqualifies, licentiousness and idol worship disqualify: for the Merciful One juxtaposed them to a blemish, as it is written (Leviticus 22:25): “because their corruption is in them, there is a blemish in them.”
tosafot:a13.1: Wherever a blemish disqualifies, licentiousness and idol worship disqualify: everyone accepts this exposition, even the one who excludes the animal that copulated, the one that was the object of bestiality, the one set aside and the one worshipped from “from the cattle” and “from the herd” in the chapter Kol HaAsurin (Temura 28a), as I explained above in the chapter HaLokeaḥ Behema.
gershom:a13.1: Is juxtaposed: [the price of a dog] is not taught [as licentiousness itself; it is juxtaposed to the payment to a prostitute] because they are written in one verse.
rashi:a15.1: A tumtum and a hermaphrodite, it is uncertain: whether it is male or female; therefore, whichever it is, they are tithed. And Rabbi Shimon holds that it is a creature of its own kind.
gershom:a14.1: He holds it is uncertain: and whichever way, whether it is male or female, it is obligated in tithe.
tosafot:a16.1: A definite male, a definite female, but not a tumtum, etc.: this passage does not follow Rav Ḥisda and Reish Lakish, as I explained above at the end of Al Elu Mumin (Bekhorot 42b).
rashi:a18.1: These too should not: one born by caesarean section, one whose time has not arrived, and an orphan.
tosafot:a18.1: Excluding a tereifa, which does not pass: for an animal whose legs were cut off from the knee upward is one of the eighteen tereifot. And there, in Menaḥot (6a), three verses are needed for a tereifa: one for an animal that was a tereifa from its mother’s womb, which never had a time of fitness; one for an animal that became a tereifa and was afterward consecrated; and one for an animal that was consecrated and afterward became a tereifa. An animal cut from the knee downward we count as one that passes, since it is not a tereifa.
rashi:b1.1: Is a full-fledged offspring: in Tractate Nidda, in the chapter Yotzei Dofen (Nidda 40a), Rabbi Shimon says that it counts as born and its mother is impure with the impurity of childbirth, and Reish Lakish explains the reason there in the Gemara: “she shall bear” includes one born by caesarean section. So here too we say: “when it is born” includes one born by caesarean section.
rashi:b1.2: And not in accordance with Rabbi Yoḥanan: who says there, in that same chapter, that Rabbi Shimon concedes with regard to consecrated animals that it is not sanctified, since he derives “birth,” “birth” from the firstborn, which requires [the opening of] the womb.
gershom:b1.1: With regard to one born by caesarean section, he holds like Rabbi Shimon, who says in Tractate Nidda that it is a full-fledged offspring, as it is written, “and if she bears a female,” to include one born by caesarean section.
gershom:b2.1: And not in accordance with Rabbi Yoḥanan: who disagrees with him there and says that Rabbi Shimon concedes with regard to consecrated animals that it is not sanctified, since it is not an offspring.
rashi:b2.1: Like Rabbi Shimon [so Rashi’s heading; the printed Gemara reads Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda]: who says that it enters the pen to be tithed, as we explained his statement above in the chapter HaLokeaḥ Behema Min HaOved Kokhavim (Bekhorot 21b).
rashi:b2.2: And the shelaḥ: and the hide exists when the offspring comes out.
gershom:b3.1: With regard to one whose time has not arrived, he holds like Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda, who said above that one whose time has not arrived enters the pen to be tithed, and it is like a firstborn, etc.
rashi:b3.1: Ben Satriel of Arkat Leveina: a place.
rashi:b3.2: The dead one: when [the mother] has a hard labor because of the offspring, they flay the hide of the mother, who is dead, and clothe the offspring, which is alive, with it, and it survives because of what they do for it.
rashi:b3.3: The living one: this is the offspring.
rashi:b3.4: The reason of our mishna is revealed: surely this is why Rabbi Yehoshua says that if it was born while the hide exists it is not an orphan: since the hide benefits the offspring, it is as though its mother were still there.
gershom:b4.1: From Arkat Leveina. They flay the dead one, her hide, and clothe the living one, the orphan.
gershom:b5.1: The reason of our mishna is revealed: that of Rabbi Yehoshua. [A bracketed editorial note proposes reading: surely, since they treat it this way, that is why Rabbi Yehoshua holds so.] And when they do this to it, it lives.
rashi:b4.1: And he further testified this: the ḥazeirin in our locale: a term for ḥazeret, a vegetable (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:b4.2: In the beit hamesses: these are the small leaves, like the flesh itself, that are in an animal’s omasum (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:b4.3: And he further testified this: once, etc., over its edge: over its side, across its width, which was so thick that sixteen wagons passed over it side by side; “over its edge” means across the width of the tree.
gershom:b6.1: Ḥazeirim: layers of leaves, as on a single stalk.
rashi:b5.1: Bar yokhani: it is a bird, as we say in several places, “like the egg of the bar yokhani.”
rashi:b5.2: Drowned: with what was inside it.
rashi:b5.3: But isn’t it written: “The wing of the renanim rejoices [ne’elasa]”: this is interpreted as an acronym: nosei, oleh venitḥatei, “carries, rises and lowers.” For so the Holy One, Blessed be He, said: Did I not create praiseworthy wings for that bird, the bar yokhani, which has so much strength that it carries an egg as large as this, lifts it up, and lowers it gently into its nest? Evidently it does not throw it down. Nitḥatei is a term for lowering, and its parallel is in Tractate Ta’anit (19a): “like a son who acts endearingly [mitḥatei] before his father.”
rashi:b5.4: It was muzarta (Rashi adds an Old French gloss): an egg that was not fit to become a chick; therefore it threw it down.
gershom:b7.1: Ne’elasa: and in Menaḥot we read, “carries, rises and lowers”: that is, it carries and raises its egg, and lowers it and sets it in its nest. When it wants to lay its egg, it goes down to the ground and lays it gently, as it is said, “for she leaves her eggs on the earth.” Evidently it does not throw it down so that it would break.
gershom:b8.1: That one which fell was unfertilized, so it did not care about it.
rashi:b6.1: Mishna. Three gathering times [literally, threshing floors] for animal tithe: that is, at three seasons in the year comes the time of animal tithe. The animals born to him between one season and the next he must tithe when the season arrives, for once the season arrives he may not eat of them in the first place without tithing, by rabbinic law; before that it is permitted. Tithing one’s animals is a mitzva in itself, and the tenth is sacred once he has called it by that name, but he is free to eat [them] without tithing. At these three times, however, the Sages required him not to eat [them] in the first place without tithing. The Gemara explains what is special about these times and why the mishna uses the term “threshing floors.”
rashi:b6.2: Adjacent [peras]: the Gemara explains how long that is. And the reasons of all these tanna’im are explained in the Gemara.
rashi:b6.3: And those are the gathering times for animal tithe: when the animals are tevel [forbidden until tithed] by rabbinic law.
tosafot:b6.1: In brief: “Adjacent to Passover” is explained in the Gemara as fifteen days: peras means half (perusa) of the thirty days in which one studies the laws of Passover before Passover. Ben Azzai’s twenty-ninth of Adar does not disagree with Rabbi Akiva, since the Adar next to Nisan is always short, so his date always falls fifteen days before Passover, which shows that the eve of Passover is counted among the fifteen. Rosh HaShana 7a implies the same about Purim and the thirty days, and Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon’s first of Nisan follows the view of two weeks, again counting the eve of Passover. The difficulty: why then do Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon move from the first of Tishrei to the twenty-ninth of Elul, when by that count the second of Tishrei should do, with the first day of Sukkot counting like the eve of Passover? Tosafot weigh sources on what the study before a festival is for (Avoda Zara 5b, Pesaḥim 6b, Megilla 29b) and answer: the day itself is never counted; the Sages did not distinguish between Passover and Sukkot, but counted the two weeks from the first of Nisan and the first of Tishrei, following the main festival day with its many offerings. Similarly, they fixed the announcement of the shekels on the first of Adar without moving it a day earlier to make a full thirty days. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:b9.1: Three gathering times for tithe: that is, three times in the year they set aside animal tithe: adjacent to Passover, etc.
rashi:b7.1: And one cannot tithe on a Festival: as the Gemara explains, because of the red paint, since the tenth must be marked with red paint, and on a Festival that is impossible because it is dyeing.
gershom:b10.1: And why did they not say the first of Tishrei: that is, since they hold that the first of Tishrei is the new year for animal tithe, as stated in the Gemara.
rashi:b8.1: The new year: those born before it do not enter the pen to be tithed together with those born from then on, because they are new and old.
rashi:b8.2: The Elul-born: those born in Elul are tithed neither with those of Tishrei nor with those of Av. The Gemara explains the reason: he is uncertain whether the halakha follows Rabbi Meir, or Rabbi Shimon, who holds the first of Tishrei; therefore they are tithed by themselves.
rashi:b9.1: All those born, etc.: now we have come to Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon, who say that the first of Tishrei is the new year for animal tithe.
rashi:b9.2: Join: to be gathered into one pen.
rashi:b9.3: Before the gathering time: one of these three gathering times, for a gathering time does not divide them.
rashi:b9.4: Why were they stated: for what halakha?
rashi:b9.5: To sell and to slaughter: in the first place, without tithing.
rashi:b10.1: Gemara. To collect the ḥurfei, the aflei and the kaytei: some animals give birth early, before Passover; some are late, giving birth between Passover and Atzeret [Shavuot]; and some do not give birth until between Atzeret and the Festival [Sukkot]. Corresponding to them the Sages instituted these times: the ḥurfei adjacent to Passover, the aflei adjacent to Atzeret, the kaytei adjacent to the Festival. Some read: the kaytei adjacent to Atzeret and the aflei adjacent to the Festival.
gershom:b11.1: To collect the ḥurfei, the aflei and the kaytei: the early ones conceive in Tishrei and give birth in Nisan, and they are tithed close to their birth; the late ones give birth in Tishrei, that is, adjacent to the Festival; and the kaytei give birth in the summer, adjacent to Atzeret.
gershom:b12.1: And why is their gathering at these particular times?
